claim: Equixly's security assessment of popular MCP server implementations found 43% contained command injection vulnerabilities, 22% allowed path traversal/arbitrary file read, 30% permitted unrestricted SSRF-style URL fetching, and 5% had other security issues.
stance_target: the Model Context Protocol tool ecosystem used in multi-agent software-factory architectures is secure by default
scope_conditions: Equixly security research, approximately one month of MCP server assessments, published March 29, 2025
quoted_support: Command Injection Vulnerabilities: 43% of tested implementations contained command injection flaws. Path Traversal/Arbitrary File Read: 22% allowed accessing files outside intended directories. SSRF Vulnerabilities: 30% permitted unrestricted URL fetching. Other Security Issues: 5% had miscellaneous security concerns.

claim: When Equixly disclosed MCP server vulnerabilities to development teams, only 30% acknowledged and released fixes, 45% dismissed the risks as 'theoretical' or 'acceptable,' and 25% did not respond to the disclosure at all.
stance_target: adversarial model review and rigid evals must not rely on vendor self-remediation of discovered tool/MCP-server vulnerabilities, since most do not fix promptly
quoted_support: 30% acknowledged and released fixes. 45% claimed the security risks were "theoretical" or "acceptable"... 25% did not respond to our security disclosures.

claim: The MCP protocol specification mandates session identifiers directly in URLs (GET /messages/?sessionId=UUID), exposing them in server logs and creating a session-hijacking vector that is a protocol-level flaw, not an implementation bug that can be patched by individual server authors.
stance_target: blast-radius mitigation for agent tool protocols requires addressing protocol-level security design flaws, not just per-server hardening
scope_conditions: Model Context Protocol specification analysis, Equixly, 2025
quoted_support: Session IDs in URLs: The protocol specification mandates session identifiers in URLs (GET /messages/?sessionId=UUID), which fundamentally violates security best practices. This design exposes sensitive identifiers in logs and a session could be hijacked by an attacker.

claim: MCP servers can be invoked directly by any caller, not only by LLMs following plan/act transparency conventions, which expands the practical attack surface beyond what most implementers have secured against.
stance_target: the zero-hallucination/blast-radius pillar must account for the agent tool layer being independently attackable, not just the LLM's own decision-making
quoted_support: MCP servers can be called by anyone, not just LLMs. While LLMs typically show what they're going to do with "plan" and "act" phases, a malicious attacker has no such transparency. This creates an expanded attack surface that many developers haven't properly secured.
